author: Steam Discovery Research
methodology: Game-first editorial synthesis of public developer accounts, practitioner case studies and dated Steam observations. These are not our interviews or audited campaign accounts. Observed facts, reported claims and proposed experiments are distinguished; missing spend, sales and attribution remain unknown.

stories.title: DREADMOOR
stories.headline: Sell a recognizable fear, then prove there is a game underneath
stories.deck: Fishing offers a readable ritual; threatening water gives it tension. Repeated playable proof matters as much as a striking trailer.
stories.releaseStatus: Unreleased; Steam lists Q4 2026 as a planned window.
stories.marketQuestion: Can a familiar activity make an unfamiliar horror world easier to understand?
stories.playerPromise: Risk another catch, improve your vessel and return alive from an unsettling flooded world.
stories.hook: A routine fishing action becomes a decision about greed, safety and preparation.

story.heading: The product behind the attention
story.body: Our interpretation: fishing is an unusually legible entry point. A viewer understands a line, a catch and a boat without learning a fictional economy. Horror changes the meaning of that ordinary task: staying longer may improve the haul while making the return more dangerous. The useful design question is whether a player feels that tradeoff, not whether screenshots merely resemble an established fishing hit.

story.heading: Interest, not a launch result
story.body: The campaign records below show dated interest milestones, not purchases. The later official announcement extends the story beyond the older marketing column. Treat it as a new checkpoint, not proof that the intervening showcase caused the increase. A wishlist is an expression of future interest; it does not reveal price tolerance, refund risk or whether the playable experience satisfies the trailer.

story.heading: What a small team should learn
story.body: Our inference: the strongest transferable asset is a repeatable tension-producing interaction. Build one encounter that can generate several truthful clips, then let a small test group expose where the controls or feedback break. Publishing more footage only helps if it sharpens the same promise. A spectacular reveal followed by an ordinary minigame may increase the eventual expectation gap.

kpis.caveat: Not sales.

kpis.label: Later wishlist milestone
kpis.caveat: Not today's balance or isolated showcase lift.

kpis.caveat: Unreleased; playtests are separate.

Mixed channels.

demand.audience: Players attracted to eerie exploration and tangible progression.
demand.job: Make a satisfying catch while managing uncertainty.
demand.supply: DREADMOOR itself occupies this intersection; no genre census was established.
demand.opening: Test a shorter, stronger risk/reward encounter, not a supposedly empty genre.
demand.notProven: That this audience wants your art style, price or short format.

mechanism.observed: Playtesting, social, showcases and creators accompanied wishlist spikes.
mechanism.inference: Repeated proof may reduce skepticism and make the promise memorable.
mechanism.confounds: Spend is unknown. 'Tripled' is approximate. February IGN participation precedes claimed first IGN contact in March; sequence unresolved.

buildTransfer.borrow: A familiar action with an unsettling consequence.
buildTransfer.change: Night Quota: a stationary fishing kiosk instead of a traversable flooded world.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Three catches, one upgrade and one looming threat; sell now or risk another cast. Two developers build the loop; the artist creates readable catch silhouettes. PM tests decisions; marketer captures real alternatives.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: Fixed camera region, scripted water threat, simple inventory; no sailing, land combat or multiplayer.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: DREADMOOR's names, creatures, vessel art or broad content promise.
buildTransfer.successTest: By day five, cold testers should understand why stopping can be the smart choice. By day fifteen, show two genuinely different outcomes.

risks: Atmosphere hides shallow fishing.
Scope expands into boat physics.
Reach is mistaken for purchase demand.

stories.title: Design and Conjure
stories.headline: Make the payoff visible, then find creators who already enjoy it
stories.deck: Tidying and decorating can explain themselves on video. The hard part is delivering satisfying choices rather than a pleasant asset catalogue.
stories.releaseStatus: Full game coming soon; separate demo released August 3, 2025.
stories.marketQuestion: Can a compact transformation create enough pleasure to make viewers want control?
stories.playerPromise: Restore magical spaces at a gentle pace and make them feel personal.
stories.hook: A neglected room becomes an inviting place through small player decisions.

story.heading: A promise with its own demonstration
story.body: Our interpretation: this concept connects two related pleasures—removing disorder and expressing taste. They need different feedback. Cleaning needs an unmistakable improvement; decorating needs several outcomes that feel valid. A beautiful room is not sufficient evidence of either. The decisive clip shows the player's intervention changing the space, so the viewer can imagine making a different choice.

story.heading: The campaign was also a logistics problem
story.body: The agency's useful lesson is operational: relevant creators, ready assets and quick decisions made a short campaign possible. The output and wishlist figures below describe different stages of the funnel. They are not a conversion table. Festival visibility arrived alongside sponsored coverage, and the case supplies neither a counterfactual nor a disclosed budget.

story.heading: The current product is a separate checkpoint
story.body: Steam now offers a distinct demo while the full product remains upcoming. That distinction prevents a common research error: assigning demo feedback or campaign attention to a paid launch that has not happened. For this team, the next useful proof is behavioral. Do unfamiliar players enjoy arranging the room after the required task ends, or are they only completing instructions?

kpis.caveat: Fifteen creators approached.

kpis.caveat: Not unique viewers.

kpis.caveat: Includes festival promotion.

kpis.caveat: Demo app 3641540; 99% positive. Not full-game purchasers.

demand.audience: Players seeking gentle completion and room-making.
demand.job: Turn disorder into something welcoming and personally chosen.
demand.supply: Decorating is a recognizable promise; this case provides no supply denominator.
demand.opening: Give each furnishing a playful purpose, not merely another visual variant.
demand.notProven: Whether a new audience values your specific theme enough to buy.

mechanism.observed: Matched cozy creators delivered sponsored content during a festival.
mechanism.inference: Audience fit and visible transformation may lower explanation costs.
mechanism.confounds: Dates, total spend and incremental lift are unknown; views cannot be divided into a valid conversion rate.

buildTransfer.change: Rooms for Odd Tenants: furnish one tiny room for an oversized snail with unusual needs.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Six props, two room conditions and several valid layouts. Developers implement placement and feedback; artist makes one expressive tenant. PM watches uncoached play; marketer tests a transformation clip.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: One room, authored sockets, simple tenant reactions; no thousand-item catalogue, branching story or town.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: The witch characters, branded room designs or implied breadth.
buildTransfer.successTest: By day five, players understand the tenant's needs; by day fifteen, they voluntarily try a second layout. This is an internal test, not a market benchmark.

risks: Decoration offers no meaningful choice.
Placement feels fiddly.
A cozy label conceals a large art workload.

stories.title: Hauntii
stories.headline: A better pitch can unlock funding without proving a sales breakout
stories.deck: Possession and atmosphere explain a distinctive adventure more clearly than a control-scheme label. Commercial outcomes still need separate evidence.
stories.releaseStatus: Released May 23, 2024. Current Steam publisher: Balor Games; historical case: Firestoke.
stories.marketQuestion: What changes when marketing describes the player's power instead of the genre's inputs?
stories.playerPromise: Become parts of a strange world to solve problems and uncover a ghost's past.
stories.hook: The environment is not merely scenery; it can become something you control.

story.heading: Reframe the experience, not the evidence
story.body: Our interpretation: calling a game a twin-stick shooter tells a practiced audience how it controls, but may leave everyone else expecting a reflex challenge. A possession-led promise instead raises a concrete question: what can I become, and what does that let me do? The lesson is not to hide combat. It is to choose the explanation that best represents the experience players actually receive.

story.heading: A funding story with a visible limit
story.body: GIYA describes recovering from failed crowdfunding through positioning and publisher-pitch work, ending in a Firestoke agreement. That establishes a reported financing outcome, not the game's lifetime economics. The later Steam footprint below is useful precisely because it resists an easy success narrative. Neither a modest Steam peak nor positive reviews settles profitability: budget, contract terms and other-platform results are missing.

story.heading: The build must make the sentence true
story.body: Our inference: a strong verb can organize development as well as copy. If the pitch is possession, each early obstacle should reveal a new consequence of controlling an object. A short slice can test that proposition without recreating an expansive world. Attractive presentation helps people notice it, but only an enjoyable sequence of decisions tests whether the promise has substance.

demand.opening: Build around one versatile verb with unmistakable consequences.

mechanism.inference: A clearer promise can align audience expectations and production decisions.

buildTransfer.borrow: One power that transforms familiar objects into tools.
buildTransfer.change: Night Shift for Furniture: a tiny ghost operates a fan, lamp and trolley to finish one absurd delivery.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Three controllable props and three linked obstacles in one room. Developers implement a shared possession interface; artist makes transformations readable. PM observes discovery; marketer compares verb-led and genre-led footage.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: Authored interactions, fixed camera and resettable states; no universal possession or large combat roster.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: Hauntii's ghost design, two-tone compositions or world-building.
buildTransfer.successTest: By day five, players discover a second use without instructions. By day fifteen, a cold viewer can explain the power from actual gameplay.

risks: The hook is only cosmetic.
Each object requires expensive bespoke code.
Funding is advertised as consumer-market validation.

stories.title: Into the Radius VR
stories.headline: Shared audiences can create distribution; impressions still are not buyers
stories.deck: A specialist VR survival game found promotional partners around a common player interest. The transferable lesson is audience fit, not guaranteed Steam featuring.
stories.releaseStatus: Full release July 20, 2020; Early Access began November 6, 2019.
stories.marketQuestion: Can complementary games make a niche audience easier to reach together?
stories.playerPromise: Prepare carefully, handle equipment physically and survive an uncertain expedition.
stories.hook: Ordinary equipment procedures become tense when performed inside a hostile world.

story.heading: Demand comes from the procedure
story.body: Our interpretation: this fantasy is not simply shooting at threats. Packing, handling equipment and deciding whether to continue an expedition can make players feel competent and vulnerable simultaneously. VR gives those procedures physical presence. That matters when borrowing the concept: a desktop version does not automatically inherit either the embodied appeal or the same addressable audience.

story.heading: The event was a coalition
story.body: CM Games' historical postmortem describes matching VR-action participants, coordinating promotional material and receiving substantial Steam placement. Its exposure figures cover different surfaces. A person may encounter both repeatedly, so adding them into a unique-audience number is invalid. The useful mechanism is a relevant recommendation context; the unknown is how much additional purchasing the collaboration caused.

story.heading: Transfer the fit, not the scale
story.body: Our inference: a small team should identify neighboring audiences before pursuing a large event. A useful partner has players who would understand the prototype's central pleasure, not merely a large following. The current developer site still invites giveaway collaboration, but an invitation route is not an endorsement or guaranteed placement. For the sprint, a reliable build and appropriate partners are controllable; platform featuring is not.

demand.job: Feel prepared while deciding how much danger to accept.

demand.opening: Test a compact equipment dilemma with a sharply different setting.

mechanism.inference: Curation may make discovery more relevant and reduce explanation effort.

buildTransfer.borrow: Preparation that visibly changes survival options.
buildTransfer.change: Anomaly Parcel Service: carry one unstable package across a small industrial yard.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Three tools, one route fork and one threat. Developers build equipment states and recovery; artist establishes readable hazards. PM tests decisions; marketer checks whether the procedure is watchable.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: Desktop-first unless an established VR foundation exists; one authored area, slot inventory, no full weapon simulation.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: The setting, branded equipment presentation or assumption that VR demand transfers.
buildTransfer.successTest: By day five, choosing a tool changes the route. By day fifteen, testers can explain their tradeoff and retry without coaching.

risks: Interaction friction replaces meaningful decisions.
VR scope consumes the sprint.
Exposure is mistaken for profitable demand.

stories.title: Dear Passengers
stories.headline: The airline fantasy attracted attention; the repeatable game still has to earn it
stories.deck: A huge wishlist story is strongest as evidence of an appealing promise—not proof that any chaotic co-op clone will sell.
stories.releaseStatus: Unreleased; Steam displays a planned 2026 release as checked on 2026-09-03.
stories.marketQuestion: What makes a familiar job feel like a game friends will want to sabotage together?
stories.playerPromise: Crew an unreliable airline, make questionable decisions, and turn your friends' mistakes into the evening's shared story.
stories.hook: A serious public-service role collides with permission to behave irresponsibly.

story.heading: What actually happened
story.body: FLEXUS publicly reported one million wishlists in its July milestone announcement and two million later that month. The game is still unreleased, so those numbers describe anticipation, not paying customers. Its store makes the intended loop more concrete: choose passengers and cargo, fly, service the cabin, and manage escalating problems. Lieu's comparison with Banana Airways favors the readable, playful incidents, but explicitly refuses to explain the campaigns' view gap through editing alone.

story.heading: Why the promise is worth studying
story.body: Interpretation: the useful unit of design is not an airplane; it is a social disagreement with a visible consequence. A player accepts risky cargo for a better reward, another tries to keep passengers happy, and a third interrupts both. That produces roles viewers can understand without knowing a class system. The development opportunity is to make one such collision repeatable. A funny trailer incident is weaker evidence if a normal group cannot recreate its underlying conditions during ordinary play.

story.heading: Where a copy would become expensive
story.body: Editorial recommendation: borrow the conflicting priorities, not the vehicle. A fixed room with one public-facing job and one reckless shortcut is a cheaper hypothesis to test than a flying multiplayer physics environment. Prototype the consequence first, then ask whether people deliberately create a second variation. Allocate the artist to readable poses, silhouettes, and reactions; allocate one developer to the interaction and another to the resettable session. The PM recruits cold groups while marketing captures actual play. Do not spend the final week building unrelated gag props to disguise an unfinished loop.

demand.job: Give the group an understandable task and stories worth retelling.

buildTransfer.change: Move to a fixed roadside booth or service counter with an original consequence.

Networked chaos can exhaust the production budget.

stories.title: Sheepherds!
stories.headline: A clear mechanic is more useful than a bigger list of cozy features
stories.deck: This is a 2025 release with a 2026 trailer retrospective—not a newly discovered 2026 breakout.
stories.genre: Cozy co-op herding / spatial party puzzle
stories.releaseStatus: Released on Steam on 2025-11-17; ongoing updates observed in 2026.
stories.marketQuestion: Can a relaxing game show enough friction to make the viewer want to take control?
stories.playerPromise: Be a sheepdog, guide a colorful flock, and enjoy cooperation without a mandatory time limit.
stories.hook: One familiar action—herding—creates visible spatial puzzles when colors and terrain interact.

story.heading: The campaign has a real chronology
story.body: The developer announced an IGN-exclusive launch trailer on November 15, 2025, before the November 17 release. Lieu's August 2026 article looks back at his consultation: demonstrate basic herding before adding color rules and cosmetics, and let some attempts go imperfectly. The article reports over 100,000 IGN views, but supplies no measured sales effect. A June 2026 Steam announcement later paired a new mode and key art with a summer discount.

story.heading: The commercially useful tension
story.body: Interpretation: relaxing does not need to mean visually consequence-free. The target feeling can be gentle competence: see a sheep drift away, adjust position, recover the group, and admire the result. That gives an observer a small problem to solve mentally. A trailer that immediately switches from animals to costumes loses that invitation. The useful demand hypothesis is therefore more specific than cozy co-op: approachable coordination where errors are funny, reversible, and comprehensible to spectators. The measured review footprint supports studying the execution, not declaring a large unserved market.

story.heading: A small team's version
story.body: Editorial recommendation: prototype a new herd-like object whose behavior is legible with almost no text. For example, guide wandering shopping carts into bays while wind and slopes interfere. Keep one interaction verb and one spatial rule that transforms the task. The artist can emphasize direction, state, and reactions instead of producing collectible outfits. One developer implements steering and collision; the other builds the compact challenge and reset. The PM tests whether players enjoy recovering from mistakes. Marketing should capture an understandable attempt, not only a flawless one.

kpis.caveat: 366 positive plus 6 negative. Broader than the store's displayed review subset; not sales.

kpis.caveat: Concurrency is not lifetime reach.

kpis.label: Reported IGN trailer reach
kpis.caveat: Source says over 100,000; no matched before/after conversion study.

kpis.caveat: Founding headcount, not verified current staffing or a production-duration benchmark.

timeline.outcome: Trailer distribution documented; incremental reach unreported.

demand.audience: Hypothesis: couples, families, and mixed-skill friends who want gentle coordination.
demand.job: Create shared competence without punishing the least experienced participant.
demand.trigger: The viewer understands an almost-successful attempt and imagines improving it.
demand.supply: This is an existing cozy co-op product; no complete tagged competitor cohort was counted.
demand.opening: An original, familiar task with reversible errors may distinguish a compact demo more clearly than extra cosmetics.
demand.notProven: The case does not establish a 100,000–200,000-owner opportunity or an editing-to-sales conversion.

mechanism.observed: The documented edit introduces the core action before its complications.
mechanism.inference: Readable recovery may create participation desire even without pressure or lethal failure.
mechanism.confounds: IGN distribution, price promotions, art, release timing, and content updates complicate attribution.

buildTransfer.borrow: A single action with visible state changes and recoverable mistakes.
buildTransfer.change: Invent a different object behavior and setting; do not reskin the sheep and flowers.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Proposed: three short layouts built from one room kit and two interacting rules.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: No hub, collectible catalog, online networking, procedural levels, or multiple bonus modes.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: Avoid requiring bespoke animation or realistic flock simulation before testing the spatial decision.
buildTransfer.successTest: Proposed gate: four of five cold viewers explain the rule silently, and players voluntarily retry a failed arrangement.

risks: Readable herding still needs convincing movement.
Cozy tone can conceal weak decisions.
A five-person founding team does not imply a 15-day full-game scope.

stories.title: Dosa Divas
stories.headline: Distinctive identity can clarify a pitch without proving a large market
stories.deck: Cooking, family conflict, and tactical combat form a coherent promise—but current Steam engagement remains modest.
stories.releaseStatus: Released on Steam on 2026-04-14; a demo is available on the store.
stories.marketQuestion: When several mechanics share one theme, can the audience understand why they belong together?
stories.playerPromise: Cook for communities and fight a fast-food empire through a story about estranged sisters and reconciliation.
stories.hook: Food is not merely a crafting resource; it links the characters' conflict, battles, and community recovery.

story.heading: The strong pitch and the measured footprint
story.body: The official game presents a narrative RPG in which cooking, combat, and rebuilding community connect. Lieu's consultation made the antagonist and objective clearer in the announcement trailer instead of replacing the whole edit. However, his article reports no commercial uplift. By this check, SteamDB shows 67 total reviews and an all-time peak of 20 concurrent players. Those figures do not settle cross-platform sales, profitability, or artistic value; they do prevent treating this as demonstrated mass Steam demand.

story.heading: What the niche actually asks of a developer
story.body: Interpretation: a hybrid pitch needs a unifying reason, not simply more verbs. A player who likes cooking may not automatically want tactical battles, while an RPG player may not care about food preparation. The connecting motivation has to make both actions feel necessary. That is the opportunity to test: does one culturally specific conflict turn two familiar mechanics into a more memorable whole? It is also the scope warning. If the promise relies on many villages, relationships, recipes, and animated scenes, a clear trailer can advertise a project the team cannot afford to finish.

story.heading: Transfer the connection, not the RPG
story.body: Editorial recommendation: build one encounter where the same preparation choice changes both a character's response and the mechanical outcome. For example, a tiny community kitchen could serve one demanding visitor while a single neighborhood dispute unfolds. Use authored state changes rather than a full reputation simulation. Put the before-and-after consequence on screen. The artist makes one room feel inhabited; the PM tests the motivation; marketing checks whether strangers describe the goal without being coached. If viewers only remember attractive food, the story connection is not yet doing commercial work.

kpis.label: SteamDB total reviews
kpis.caveat: 65 positive plus 2 negative; not an owner or revenue count.

kpis.label: All-time Steam peak
kpis.caveat: Steam only; do not extrapolate total platform sales.

kpis.label: Advertised demo length
kpis.caveat: Described as the first hour and a half; not observed median playtime.

kpis.label: Trailer-attributed commercial lift
kpis.caveat: Qualitative clarity is not a measured acquisition result.

timeline.action: Publish cooking-and-delivery footage and accessibility/usability fixes.
timeline.outcome: Demo save carryover to the full game was advertised.
timeline.caveat: The announcement describes features, not measured conversion.

timeline.action: Explain the announcement trailer's narrative revisions.
timeline.caveat: Displayed publication date; not the original announcement date.
Campaign budget and revenue were not disclosed in checked sources.

demand.audience: Hypothesis: narrative-RPG players attracted to a specific cultural perspective and relationships.
demand.job: Make progression emotionally meaningful rather than a sequence of disconnected systems.
demand.trigger: The player understands who needs help, who opposes them, and why the next action matters.
demand.supply: The checked material establishes a distinctive hybrid, not the number or success rate of competing hybrids.
demand.opening: Test a small, specific narrative-mechanical connection before financing an expansive content pipeline.
demand.notProven: Neither thematic originality nor positive reviews demonstrates a large reachable Steam audience.

mechanism.observed: The trailer consultation ties activities to a clearer antagonist and objective.
mechanism.inference: A unified motivation may improve recall and help the correct audience self-select.
mechanism.confounds: No exposure-controlled test; platform mix, price, distribution, timing, and audience fit remain unresolved.

buildTransfer.borrow: One visible action that changes both a relationship and a practical outcome.
buildTransfer.change: Use your team's own grounded setting and conflict; research the community you depict.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Proposed: one visitor, two preparations, one dispute, and a visible resolution in ten minutes.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: No party roster, world map, full combat system, branching campaign, or voiced cinematics.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: Do not imitate culturally specific surface details while removing the meaning that connects them.
buildTransfer.successTest: Proposed gate: cold players explain why their preparation mattered and request a second encounter for its consequence, not only its appearance.

risks: A coherent pitch may still have limited demand.
Narrative and animation multiply content cost.
A long reference demo is not a suitable 15-day target.

stories.title: Freerunners
stories.headline: A tiny movement loop can still become a years-long production trap
stories.deck: This downside case joins a modest festival result to a later release and a developer's frank account of commercial disappointment.
stories.releaseStatus: Released on Steam on 2026-03-04; the store also offers a demo.
stories.marketQuestion: Does a movement fantasy remain compelling when compressed into both a short clip and a first-time player's hands?
stories.playerPromise: Read obstacles, preserve momentum, and improve the rhythm of a clean parkour route.
stories.hook: The satisfaction is the transition between obstacles, not the inventory of moves.

story.heading: Follow the game beyond the festival headline
story.body: The 2024 festival postmortem reports limited traction and leaves conflicting wishlist arithmetic and visit totals. The later game did ship in March 2026. Rowbotham's April production retrospective says it was not a financial success and describes scope and workflow problems. Crucially, this is not a forecast reconstructed from reviews: the developer himself distinguishes the learning value of finishing from the commercial result. The small current SteamDB footprint supplies context, not an explanation for failure.

story.heading: Presentation and implementation meet at the camera
story.body: A March update changed the camera from following the pelvis bone to following the actor capsule, while early speed, stamina, and obstacle spacing were adjusted. Interpretation: for a movement game, the camera is part of the product promise. Marketing cannot repair a sensation the opening does not deliver. Conversely, an expressive animation is not useful if its camera response makes motion appear hesitant. The test should join clip comprehension and hands-on feel: can the same short route look fluid, teach itself, and reward a second attempt?

story.heading: A practical 15-day investment test
story.body: Editorial recommendation: timebox a single ninety-second route with three reusable obstacles. One developer owns movement and camera; the other builds reset, timing, and lightweight instrumentation. The artist controls silhouettes and contact cues instead of creating another district. The PM records where new players lose flow. Marketing recruits outside the team's immediate circle and uses the exported, compressed video—not only the pristine editor capture. If the route cannot earn voluntary retries, additional levels are a liability. Decide at the end of the sprint whether to continue, narrow the concept, or stop; a finished prototype is useful evidence even when the answer is no.

stories.title: Inkbound
stories.headline: Co-op changes the audience contract, not just the player count
stories.deck: A tactical roguelike reached a meaningful Steam audience while exposing design and business tensions that a short demo must decide early.
stories.releaseStatus: Steam Early Access began 2023-05-22; version 1.0 released 2024-04-09.
stories.marketQuestion: Can a cooperative strategy hook serve solo players equally without diluting what makes cooperation interesting?
stories.playerPromise: Draft a powerful build and solve tactical encounters at a pace the group can control.
stories.hook: Players can act simultaneously in turn-based battles rather than wait through a fixed teammate order.

story.heading: A real audience, with a split inside it
story.body: Shiny Shoe's postmortem reports that approximately 60% of runs were solo and 40% co-op. These are session observations, not percentages of unique customers. Cooke describes tensions between the two audiences, negative reactions to optional cosmetic monetization, and missing Chinese support as the leading Early Access refund reason. Current SteamDB engagement is substantially larger than the small-release cases here, but none of those facts quantifies which individual decision created sales or refunds.

story.heading: The demand structure is the design problem
story.body: Interpretation: co-op strategy promises conversation, shared plans, and a reason to care about another person's build. Solo strategy promises control, pace, and no dependence on a partner's availability. Some systems serve both; others require choosing. A two-person action that is essential to the hook may become meaningless when an AI partner performs it automatically. The useful opening is not adding multiplayer to a familiar roguelike, but identifying a decision that is better specifically because another person has agency. That claim should be tested before content or networking infrastructure expands.

story.heading: What can fit into a demo sprint
story.body: Editorial recommendation: use one authored encounter to investigate cooperative decision-making. Begin with two local inputs or explicit hot-seat roles so the interaction can be evaluated without a service backend. A second developer can explore networking only after the interaction proves essential and only if the team already has reliable foundations. The artist makes intent and consequences readable; the PM records disagreements and dead time; marketing tests whether the interaction is explainable in a short clip. If solo is also promised, test it separately rather than averaging both groups into one satisfaction score.

demand.audience: Hypothesis: buildcraft-focused strategy players and groups seeking tactical coordination.
demand.job: Create interesting decisions without long periods of inactive waiting.
demand.trigger: A teammate's choice enables an outcome neither player could create alone.
demand.supply: Inkbound is an established example of the hybrid, not proof of an empty co-op roguelike niche.
demand.opening: Test one genuinely interdependent decision for a clearly chosen play mode.
demand.notProven: Public data cannot price the addressable niche or show that this model transfers to a tiny unknown studio.

mechanism.observed: Simultaneous actions are advertised, and the studio documents conflicting solo/co-op feedback.
mechanism.inference: Reducing waiting may help cooperation, but preserving agency matters more than simply allowing simultaneous input.
mechanism.confounds: Prior studio reputation, Early Access iteration, localization, content depth, and business-model changes overlap.

buildTransfer.borrow: Visible intentions, complementary abilities, and immediate feedback on combined choices.
buildTransfer.change: Choose co-op-first or solo-first explicitly; do not promise equal support by default.
buildTransfer.miniDemo: Proposed: two roles, three abilities each, one arena, and three encounter variations.
buildTransfer.technicalCut: No social hub, centralized hosting fleet, procedural campaign, hundreds of items, or cosmetic shop.
buildTransfer.doNotCopy: Free testers' approval does not validate a paid business model or localization priorities.
buildTransfer.successTest: Proposed gate: cold pairs discuss meaningful choices, retain individual agency, and request another encounter; test solo satisfaction separately.

risks: Dual-mode support can double balancing obligations.
Network services add operational work beyond gameplay.
A mature studio's reach is not an attainable baseline.
